country.name: Croatia
country.tagline: Zinfandel's homeland, cliff-hung Plavac Mali, island whites with Greek roots, and the Graševina plains of Slavonia.

stats.note: Vineyard area: Eurostat apro_cpsh1, 19.1 kha in 2025. Production: 458,000 hl in 2024 (OIV figure as reported by Wine Plus).

country.overview:
Croatia is two wine countries joined at the hip. Along the Adriatic, Istria and Dalmatia are Mediterranean: limestone, sun, sea light and a thousand islands, with native grapes that taste of herbs and salt. Inland, the Pannonian plain and the hills around Zagreb are Central European: cool nights, loess and marl, and crisp whites led by Graševina (Welschriesling). Wines of Croatia divides the country into four regions: Istria and Kvarner, Dalmatia, the Croatian Uplands and Slavonia with the Croatian Danube. Under EU law there are 18 wine PDOs: three broad regional names (Eastern Continental, Western Continental and Coastal Croatia), twelve subregions such as Hrvatska Istra, Slavonija and Srednja i Južna Dalmacija, and three small site appellations: Dingač, Ponikve and Muškat momjanski.

The vineyard area is about 19,000 ha and falling slowly, and production is around 0.4 to 0.5 million hl. Most farms are tiny, and Croatians drink the bulk of their wine at home, which helps explain why Croatian wine prices are high for the region. The industry has been rebuilt since the 1991 to 1995 war, which hit the Danube vineyards around Vukovar and Ilok especially hard, and since EU entry in 2013 a generation of small estates has emerged on the coast and in Slavonia.

The coastal grapes are the treasure. Plavac Mali, the great red of Dalmatia, grows on vertiginous south-facing slopes such as Dingač and Postup on the Pelješac peninsula, where it ripens to 15% alcohol or more. In 2001 a DNA team led by Carole Meredith, working with Ivan Pejić and Edi Maletić of the University of Zagreb, found that a nearly vanished Dalmatian vine, Crljenak Kaštelanski, was identical to California's Zinfandel and Italy's Primitivo, and that it was a parent of Plavac Mali. The old name Tribidrag appears in a Dalmatian record of 1444. White grapes are just as local: Pošip and Grk on Korčula, Bogdanuša on Hvar, Vugava on Vis, Maraština, Debit and Kujundžuša, and, in Istria, Malvazija Istarska, the region's emblem, along with the red Teran.

Inland, Slavonia's Graševina is the country's most planted grape. It is made fresh, oak-aged or botrytised from the hills of the 'Golden Valley' around Kutjevo, where Cistercian monks built a cellar in 1232. On the Danube, Ilok's Traminac (Gewürztraminer) has royal glamour: its 1947 vintage is said to have been served at the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II in 1953. Northern hills around Zagreb (Plešivica, Zagorje and Međimurje) make some of the country's best sparkling wines and crisp aromatic whites.

history.title: Greeks on Vis and Hvar
history.text: Greek colonists from Syracuse and Paros founded Issa (Vis) and Pharos (Stari Grad on Hvar, 384 BC). Pharos's field system, divided into parcels with stone walls and still planted with vines and olives, became the UNESCO Stari Grad Plain.

history.title: Cistercians at Kutjevo
history.text: Cistercian monks founded an abbey in the Požega valley and built the Kutjevo cellar in 1232; the valley's later name, Vallis Aurea (Golden Valley), reflects its farming wealth.

history.title: Tribidrag in the archives
history.text: A record of 1444 mentions the grape Tribidrag in Dalmatia; the Statute of Budva (1426 to 1442) had already named Cratosia (Kratošija). DNA later showed both are the variety now called Zinfandel.

history.title: Ilok's Old Cellar
history.text: Iločki podrumi dates its Old Cellar to 1450, under the Iločki (Újlaki) family; after the Ottoman era Ilok passed to the Odescalchi princes in 1697.

history.title: A Traminer for the Queen
history.text: Ilok's 1947 Traminac was reportedly served at the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II, a story the winery and the British Embassy still tell.

history.title: Dingač protected
history.text: Dingač on Pelješac became the first protected Croatian wine region; Postup followed in 1967, and in 1964 Dingač received international protection as a 'famous wine'.

history.title: The Dingač tunnel
history.text: On 29 November 1975 a 400 m tunnel through the Pelješac ridge opened, financed by the growers' cooperative, replacing donkey paths over the pass and cutting a 20 km detour to 4 km.

history.title: War on the Danube
history.text: The Croatian War of Independence devastated eastern Slavonia; Ilok was occupied and its cellars looted, and many Danube vineyards were mined or abandoned until reintegration in 1998.

history.title: Zinfandel found at Kaštela
history.text: Nine vines of Crljenak Kaštelanski in a vineyard at Kaštel Novi near Split matched Zinfandel's DNA, ending a decades-long search for the grape's European origin.

history.title: EU entry
history.text: Croatia joined the EU on 1 July 2013 and its wine PDOs were registered the same day; Ponikve (2021) and Muškat momjanski (2021) followed.

country.classification: Croatian wine law nests regions (*regije*), subregions (*podregije*), vineyard areas (*vinogorja*) and single positions (*položaji*). Under the EU system 18 names are PDOs (*zaštićena oznaka izvornosti*, ZOI): the regions Istočna kontinentalna Hrvatska, Zapadna kontinentalna Hrvatska and Primorska Hrvatska; the subregions Hrvatsko Podunavlje, Slavonija, Moslavina, Prigorje-Bilogora, Plešivica, Pokuplje, Zagorje-Međimurje, Hrvatska Istra, Hrvatsko primorje, Sjeverna Dalmacija, Srednja i Južna Dalmacija and Dalmatinska zagora; and the site appellations Dingač, Ponikve and Muškat momjanski. Labels still use the traditional quality terms *kvalitetno vino* (quality wine) and *vrhunsko vino* (premium wine), and Prädikat-style sweet categories (*kasna berba*, *izborna berba*, *izborna berba bobica*, *izborna berba prosušenih bobica*, *ledeno vino*). Prošek, the Dalmatian dried-grape dessert wine, is a traditional term whose EU protection Croatia sought from 2021, against Italian objections that it is too close to Prosecco.
country.climate_soils: The coast is Mediterranean with hot, dry summers and mild winters; the bura (bora) and jugo winds shape it, and the steepest Dalmatian slopes get reflected light from the sea. Soils are karst limestone and dolomite, terra rossa in Istria, flysch (white marl, *bijela zemlja*) in northern Istria, and sand on islands such as Korčula's Lumbarda. Inland the climate is continental; Slavonia's hills are loess, clay and marl on the Papuk, Krndija and Psunj ranges, and the Danube terraces at Ilok and Erdut are thick loess.

grapes.name: Plavac Mali
grapes.note: The main Dalmatian red, offspring of Tribidrag (Zinfandel) and Dobričić; huge, tannic, high-alcohol wines on Pelješac, Hvar and Brač.

grapes.name: Crljenak Kaštelanski / Tribidrag
grapes.note: Zinfandel/Primitivo, rediscovered at Kaštela in 2001 and now replanted along the coast.

grapes.name: Graševina
grapes.note: Welschriesling, the most planted variety, especially in Slavonia; from fresh to botrytised.

grapes.name: Malvazija Istarska
grapes.note: Istria's white emblem: saline, peachy, made fresh, oak-aged or macerated.

grapes.name: Teran
grapes.note: Istrian red with high acidity and dark fruit, close to but distinct from Slovenia's Refošk-based Teran.

grapes.name: Pošip
grapes.note: Full-bodied white from Smokvica and Čara on Korčula; Pošip Čara is often cited as the first Croatian white with protected origin.

grapes.name: Grk
grapes.note: Female-flowering white of Lumbarda on Korčula's sands, interplanted with Plavac Mali as a pollinator.

grapes.name: Babić
grapes.note: Red of Primošten and Šibenik, grown in stone-walled micro-plots on bare rock.

grapes.name: Bogdanuša, Vugava, Maraština, Debit, Kujundžuša
grapes.note: Island and hinterland whites: Hvar, Vis, the Dalmatian coast and Imotski respectively.

grapes.name: Traminac
grapes.note: Gewürztraminer, famous at Ilok and in the Danube region.

regions.name: Istria and Kvarner
regions.tagline: Heart-shaped Istria, its hill towns and red earth: Malvazija, Teran and Momjan Muscat.
regions.summary: Istria is a peninsula shared with Slovenia and Italy, and its Croatian part is the PDO Hrvatska Istra, about 3,000 to 4,000 ha today against roughly 44,000 ha in the late 19th century before phylloxera. Kvarner, the gulf and islands to the east (Krk, Cres, Rab, Pag), forms the Hrvatsko primorje PDO. Istria's emblem is Malvazija Istarska, made as a fresh, saline white, as a rich oak-aged wine or as a skin-macerated amber wine; the red is Teran, with Refošk, Merlot and Cabernet. The old Venetian hill towns of the interior (Motovun, Grožnjan, Momjan, Buje) look over vineyards of red, white and grey soils, and Momjan's sweet muscat has its own PDO. Producers include Kozlović, Matošević, Roxanich, Clai, Coronica, Trapan, Kabola, Benvenuti, Cattunar and Arman. On Krk, the native Žlahtina is the island's white, centred on Vrbnik.
regions.history: Romans, Venetians and Habsburgs all ruled Istria; under Venice its wine went across the Adriatic. After 1945 the peninsula went to Yugoslavia and many Italian-speaking families left. The 1990s and 2000s brought a revival led by small family wineries and the Istrian Malvazija Festival.
regions.terroir: Terra rossa over limestone on the west coast (warm, red-fruited wines), grey and white flysch marl (*bijela* and *siva zemlja*) in the north and centre (finer, more acid-driven whites), and karst on Kvarner's islands. Mediterranean climate, cooler and windier inland.
regions.grapes: Malvazija Istarska, Teran, Refošk, Muškat momjanski, Chardonnay, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon; Žlahtina on Krk.
regions.styles: Dry whites (fresh to macerated), Teran reds, sweet Muscat, some sparkling.
regions.classification: PDOs Hrvatska Istra, Hrvatsko primorje and Muškat momjanski (all within the regional PDO Primorska Hrvatska).

regions.name: Dalmatia
regions.tagline: Karst cliffs, island fields walled by Greeks and the wild-hearted Plavac Mali: the Adriatic's most dramatic vineyards.
regions.summary: Dalmatia stretches 400 km from Zadar to Dubrovnik and includes the islands of Brač, Hvar, Korčula, Vis, Šolta and Lastovo, the Pelješac peninsula and the karst hinterland (Dalmatinska zagora). Three subregional PDOs cover it (Sjeverna Dalmacija, Srednja i Južna Dalmacija, Dalmatinska zagora) plus the site PDOs Dingač and Ponikve on Pelješac. The red is Plavac Mali, at its most extreme on the south face of Pelješac at Dingač and Postup, where 45-degree slopes of crumbling dolomite drop straight into the sea and the vines get direct sun, reflected light from the water and radiated heat from the stones. Babić rules around Primošten and Šibenik, where vines grow in tiny walled pockets on bare limestone. The whites are island natives: Pošip and Grk on Korčula, Bogdanuša on Hvar, Vugava on Vis, Maraština and Debit along the coast, Kujundžuša around Imotski. Prošek, a sweet wine from sun-dried grapes, is the traditional dessert wine.
regions.history: Greek colonists on Vis and Hvar in the 4th century BC planted vines in the Stari Grad Plain. Venice ruled much of the coast from the 15th to 18th centuries, and Dubrovnik (Ragusa) kept its own republic and its own vineyards on Pelješac, defended by the walls of Ston. Phylloxera arrived late, in the 1890s; before that, Dalmatian wine boomed as French vineyards died, and the subsequent collapse drove emigration to California and Chile. Dingač became Croatia's first protected wine in 1961. In 2001 Crljenak Kaštelanski (Zinfandel) was rediscovered at Kaštela. Miljenko 'Mike' Grgić, the Croatian-born winemaker behind Chateau Montelena's 1973 Chardonnay that won the 1976 Judgment of Paris, returned to found Grgić Vina at Trstenik on Pelješac in 1996.
regions.terroir: Karst limestone and dolomite, terra rossa in hollows, sand at Lumbarda; very hot, dry summers, high UV, sea reflection and strong winds (bura, jugo, maestral). Dry farming on steep slopes, often with goblet-trained bush vines.
regions.grapes: Plavac Mali, Babić, Tribidrag (Crljenak Kaštelanski), Lasina, Dobričić, Plavina; Pošip, Grk, Bogdanuša, Vugava, Maraština, Debit, Kujundžuša, Cetinka.
regions.styles: Powerful reds, island whites, rosé (*opolo*), and prošek.
regions.classification: Three subregional PDOs plus Dingač and Ponikve; Postup (protected in 1967) survives as a traditional name and vineyard position within Srednja i Južna Dalmacija.

regions.name: Slavonia and Croatian Danube
regions.tagline: The Golden Valley of Graševina, Cistercian cellars and the loess terraces of the Danube at Ilok.
regions.summary: Eastern continental Croatia (PDO Istočna kontinentalna Hrvatska) splits into Slavonija (the hills around the Požega basin, Kutjevo, Orahovica, Đakovo and Slavonski Brod) and Hrvatsko Podunavlje (the Croatian Danube: Baranja, Erdut and Ilok on the Srijem ridge). Graševina is king, making everything from fresh, appley whites to oak-aged and botrytised wines; Traminac, Chardonnay, Sauvignon and Frankovka follow. Kutjevo's 'Golden Valley' (Vallis Aurea) is the heart: Kutjevo d.d. (with about 430 ha of its own vines), Krauthaker, Enjingi, Galić, Feravino and others. On the Danube, Iločki podrumi, Erdutski vinogradi and Belje work big estates on loess.
regions.history: Romans planted on the Srijem ridge (the emperor Probus, born at Sirmium, is credited with planting vines on nearby Fruška Gora). Cistercians founded Kutjevo in 1232; after the Ottomans, Jesuits and then noble families (the Turković family at Kutjevo, the Odescalchi at Ilok) rebuilt the estates. The 1990s war hit the Danube vineyards hard.
regions.terroir: Loess, clay and marl on south-facing slopes of the Papuk and Krndija hills; thick loess on the Danube terraces. Continental climate with hot summers and cold winters.
regions.grapes: Graševina, Traminac, Chardonnay, Sauvignon, Pinot Blanc, Frankovka, Zweigelt, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot.
regions.styles: Dry whites, sweet late-harvest and ice wines, reds from Frankovka and Bordeaux varieties.
regions.classification: PDOs Slavonija and Hrvatsko Podunavlje within Istočna kontinentalna Hrvatska.

regions.name: Croatian Uplands
regions.tagline: The hills around Zagreb: sparkling Plešivica, aromatic Međimurje Pušipel and Moslavina's Škrlet.
regions.summary: The Croatian Uplands (PDO Zapadna kontinentalna Hrvatska) is a ring of hill country around Zagreb divided into five subregions: Plešivica (west of Zagreb, known for traditional-method sparkling and amphora wines), Zagorje-Međimurje (the northern hills, where Pušipel, local Furmint, is the signature), Prigorje-Bilogora, Moslavina (home of the native Škrlet) and Pokuplje along the Kupa. Small family estates dominate: Tomac, Korak, Jagunić and Režek in Plešivica, Bolfan, Štampar and Cmrečnjak in Zagorje-Međimurje.
regions.history: These were Habsburg-Hungarian lands with strong German and Austrian influence; vineyards are small, often weekend plots with cottages (*klijeti*).
regions.terroir: Marl, clay and limestone hills, cooler and wetter than the east.
regions.grapes: Graševina, Pušipel (Furmint), Sauvignon, Rhine Riesling, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Škrlet, Kraljevina, Portugizac.
regions.styles: Crisp whites, sparkling wines, Portugizac nouveau, late harvest.
regions.classification: Five subregional PDOs within Zapadna kontinentalna Hrvatska.

hr-dalmatinska-zagora.name: Dalmatinska zagora
hr-dalmatinska-zagora.grapes: Kujundžuša, Trnjak, Debit, Maraština, Plavac Mali
hr-dalmatinska-zagora.summary: Dalmatinska zagora is the karst hinterland behind the coast, from Knin and Drniš to Sinj, Imotski and Vrgorac. Its higher, drier and cooler plateaus give fresher wines than the coast; Kujundžuša (Imotski) and Trnjak are the local grapes, and Debit grows around Drniš.

hr-dingac.name: Dingač
hr-dingac.summary: Dingač is Croatia's most famous red wine and its first protected wine region (1961): a steep strip of south-west-facing slopes on the Pelješac peninsula above the sea, between Trstenik and Borak, worked from the village of Potomje on the other side of the ridge. Only Plavac Mali is permitted, with a maximum of 8 t/ha. The slopes reach 45 degrees on crumbling dolomitic limestone with almost no topsoil, and the vines get sun from above, light reflected from the sea and heat radiated by the stones, so the grapes shrivel and concentrate. The wines are dark, tannic, often 15% alcohol or more, with dried fig, carob, black cherry, tobacco and herb notes. Until 1975 the grapes went over the ridge by donkey; the growers' cooperative then financed a 400 m tunnel from Potomje. The protected area covers about 758 ha, of which about 78 ha are planted.
hr-dingac.terroir: Karst dolomite and limestone scree, slopes up to 45 degrees, 0 to 300 m above the sea, extreme sun and heat; dry-farmed bush vines.
hr-dingac.nerd_note: Plavac Mali is a cross of Tribidrag (Zinfandel) and Dobričić, an old variety from the island of Šolta, so every bottle of Dingač is Zinfandel's grandchild in a sense.

hr-hrvatska-istra.name: Hrvatska Istra
hr-hrvatska-istra.grapes: Malvazija Istarska, Teran, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Refošk, Muscat
hr-hrvatska-istra.summary: Hrvatska Istra is the subregional PDO for Croatian Istria, 41 municipalities from Umag and Buje to Pula and Labin. It is Croatia's most dynamic wine region: Malvazija Istarska makes up about half the plantings, followed by Teran, Merlot, Cabernet, Refošk and Muscat. The west coast's red terra rossa gives riper, rounder wines; the grey and white marls of the interior around Motovun, Buje and Momjan give tighter whites. Producers range from the large Agrolaguna to family estates such as Kozlović, Matošević, Roxanich, Clai, Coronica, Trapan, Kabola, Benvenuti, Cattunar and Arman.
hr-hrvatska-istra.nerd_note: Croatian producers can label Teran only with 'Hrvatska Istra' alongside it, under a 2017 EU derogation that Slovenia, which holds the Teran PDO, contested.

hr-hrvatsko-podunavlje.name: Hrvatsko Podunavlje
hr-hrvatsko-podunavlje.grapes: Graševina, Traminac, Rhine Riesling, Chardonnay, Frankovka, Cabernet Sauvignon
hr-hrvatsko-podunavlje.summary: Croatian Danube covers the loess ridges along the Danube in Baranja (Zmajevac, Kneževi Vinogradi), Erdut and Srijem (Ilok). Ilok's Traminac and Graševina, from the large Iločki podrumi, are the best-known wines; Erdutski vinogradi and Belje are other major estates.

hr-hrvatsko-primorje.name: Hrvatsko primorje
hr-hrvatsko-primorje.summary: Hrvatsko primorje covers the Kvarner gulf and its islands (Krk, Cres, Lošinj, Rab, Pag) and the coast from Rijeka to Karlobag. Its best-known wine is Vrbnička Žlahtina from Vrbnik on Krk, a light, fresh, floral white from the native Žlahtina; Pag's Gegić is another island specialty.

hr-istocna-kontinentalna-hrvatska.name: Istočna kontinentalna Hrvatska
hr-istocna-kontinentalna-hrvatska.grapes: Graševina and other permitted continental varieties
hr-istocna-kontinentalna-hrvatska.summary: The regional umbrella PDO for eastern continental Croatia, covering Slavonija and Hrvatsko Podunavlje (133 municipalities), used for wines blended across the two subregions, typically larger-volume Graševina from producers who buy fruit from both Slavonia and the Danube.

hr-moslavina.name: Moslavina
hr-moslavina.summary: Moslavina is a small hill range south-east of Zagreb around Kutina and Popovača. It is the home of Škrlet, a native white with light body, citrus and herbal notes, rescued from near-extinction and now the subregion's calling card.

hr-muskat-momjanski.name: Muškat momjanski
hr-muskat-momjanski.grapes: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains (Momjan muscat)
hr-muskat-momjanski.summary: Muškat momjanski is a PDO (August 2021) for wines from Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains grown around the hilltop village of Momjan near Buje in north-west Istria. Momjan's muscat was famous in the Habsburg period; today it is made dry, off-dry and as a sweet late-harvest wine with orange-blossom and honey notes. Kozlović and Prelac are among the producers.

hr-plesivica.name: Plešivica
hr-plesivica.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Graševina, Rhine Riesling, Sauvignon, Portugizac
hr-plesivica.summary: Plešivica, a low range of hills west of Zagreb around Jastrebarsko and Samobor, is Croatia's sparkling-wine capital and one of its most forward-thinking areas. Tomac, Korak, Režek, Jagunić and Šember make traditional-method sparkling and still wines from Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Riesling, Graševina, Sauvignon and Portugizac; Tomac also ferments in buried amphorae.

hr-pokuplje.name: Pokuplje
hr-pokuplje.summary: Pokuplje follows the Kupa river south-west of Zagreb around Karlovac and Ozalj; a small, cool subregion of light whites (Graševina, Kraljevina, Chardonnay) and some Portugizac. Its scattered hillside plots are mostly family vineyards for home consumption, with only a few commercial bottlers.

hr-ponikve.name: Ponikve
hr-ponikve.summary: Ponikve, registered in February 2021 as Croatia's 17th wine PDO, is a small plateau and hamlet near Ston at the neck of the Pelješac peninsula. The PDO covers wines from Plavac Mali, Pošip and Maraština, including a style made from raisined grapes, and was created to give the locality's name visibility on labels. Ponikve's karst fields sit higher and cooler than the south-facing Dingač slopes.

hr-prigorje-bilogora.name: Prigorje-Bilogora
hr-prigorje-bilogora.summary: Prigorje-Bilogora takes in the slopes north and east of Zagreb (Zelina, Križevci, Koprivnica, Bjelovar). It makes light whites, notably Kraljevina around Sveti Ivan Zelina, plus Graševina and Pinot Gris. Zelina's Kraljevina, a pink-skinned, low-alcohol local grape, is the classic wine of Zagreb's taverns.

hr-primorska-hrvatska.name: Primorska Hrvatska
hr-primorska-hrvatska.summary: Primorska Hrvatska is the regional umbrella PDO for all of coastal Croatia (Istria, Kvarner and Dalmatia), about 180 municipalities, used for wines blended across subregions. A producer who buys Plavac Mali from Pelješac and Babić from Primošten for one wine, for instance, labels it Primorska Hrvatska; most quality wines name their subregion instead.

hr-sjeverna-dalmacija.name: Sjeverna Dalmacija
hr-sjeverna-dalmacija.grapes: Babić, Plavac Mali, Lasina, Debit, Maraština
hr-sjeverna-dalmacija.summary: Northern Dalmatia runs from Zadar to Primošten and Rogoznica, with the islands of Pašman, Ugljan and the Kornati. Its signature is Babić, a dark, firm red grown around Primošten and Šibenik in tiny vineyards hacked out of bare limestone and protected by dry-stone walls; Debit and Maraština are the whites.

hr-slavonija.name: Slavonija
hr-slavonija.grapes: Graševina, Traminac, Chardonnay, Pinot Blanc, Sauvignon, Frankovka
hr-slavonija.summary: Slavonija is the subregion of the hills ringing the Požega basin and the northern slopes toward the Drava: Kutjevo, Orahovica, Feričanci, Đakovo, Slavonski Brod, Daruvar and Pakrac. Its 'Golden Valley' around Kutjevo is Croatia's Graševina heartland, with wines from crisp and appley to oak-aged and botrytised; Traminac, Pinot Blanc, Chardonnay, Sauvignon and Frankovka also do well. Cistercians built Kutjevo's first cellar in 1232.
hr-slavonija.terroir: Loess, clay and marl on south-facing slopes of the Papuk and Krndija hills at 150 to 350 m; continental climate.

hr-srednja-i-juzna-dalmacija.name: Srednja i Južna Dalmacija
hr-srednja-i-juzna-dalmacija.grapes: Plavac Mali, Tribidrag, Pošip, Grk, Bogdanuša, Vugava, Malvasija Dubrovačka, Maraština
hr-srednja-i-juzna-dalmacija.summary: Central and Southern Dalmatia covers the coast from Trogir and Split to Dubrovnik and Konavle plus the islands of Brač, Hvar, Vis, Korčula, Šolta, Lastovo and Mljet, and Pelješac. It holds most of Croatia's great coastal wines: Plavac Mali from Pelješac (Postup, Trstenik), Hvar (Sveta Nedjelja, Ivan Dolac) and Brač; Pošip and Grk from Korčula; Bogdanuša from Hvar; Vugava from Vis; Crljenak Kaštelanski from Kaštela; and Malvasija Dubrovačka from Konavle.

hr-zagorje-medimurje.name: Zagorje, Međimurje
hr-zagorje-medimurje.grapes: Pušipel (Furmint), Sauvignon, Rhine Riesling, Graševina, Traminac, Muscat
hr-zagorje-medimurje.summary: Zagorje-Međimurje covers the hills of Hrvatsko Zagorje north of Zagreb and Međimurje between the Mura and Drava, against the Slovenian and Hungarian borders. Međimurje's steep Štrigova hills make taut, aromatic Sauvignon, Riesling and Pušipel (local Furmint), and some excellent late-harvest wines.

hr-zapadna-kontinentalna-hrvatska.name: Zapadna kontinentalna Hrvatska
hr-zapadna-kontinentalna-hrvatska.summary: The regional umbrella PDO for western continental Croatia, covering the five upland subregions (about 200 municipalities): Plešivica, Zagorje-Međimurje, Prigorje-Bilogora, Moslavina and Pokuplje. It is used for wines that blend fruit across those hills or do not qualify for a subregion name.

sites.name: Dingač vineyards
sites.text: The south face of the Pelješac ridge above the sea between Trstenik and Borak: 45-degree slopes of dolomite scree planted with bush-trained Plavac Mali. Protected since 1961, it was Croatia's first appellation. The vines bake under direct sun, reflected light from the sea and heat from the stones.

sites.name: Dingač tunnel, Potomje
sites.text: The 400 m single-lane tunnel through the Pelješac ridge opened on 29 November 1975, financed by the Potomje growers' cooperative. It replaced the donkey path over the pass and cut the trip from village to vineyard from 20 km to about 4.

sites.name: Postup
sites.text: West of Dingač near Donja Banda, Postup is another steep south-facing slope of Plavac Mali above the sea. It was protected in 1967 and is often considered slightly fresher and more elegant than Dingač.

sites.name: Grgić Vina, Trstenik
sites.text: Miljenko 'Mike' Grgić, the Croatian-born winemaker of the Chateau Montelena 1973 Chardonnay that won the 1976 Judgment of Paris, returned to his homeland in 1996 to found this winery at Trstenik on Pelješac, making Plavac Mali and Pošip.

sites.name: Kaštel Novi, Zinfandel's rediscovery
sites.text: In 2001 DNA from nine old vines of Crljenak Kaštelanski in a vineyard at Kaštel Novi, between Split and Trogir, matched California Zinfandel. The UC Davis team of Carole Meredith worked with Ivan Pejić and Edi Maletić of Zagreb. The variety, also called Tribidrag, has since been replanted around Kaštela.

sites.name: Smokvica, Korčula
sites.text: Smokvica and neighbouring Čara in the middle of Korčula are the home of Pošip, a rich, golden white said to have been found as a chance seedling in the 19th century. Their karst fields hold most of the island's Pošip.

sites.name: Lumbarda, Korčula
sites.text: On the sandy eastern tip of Korčula, Lumbarda grows Grk, a white whose flowers are functionally female, so Plavac Mali is interplanted as a pollinator. The sand, rare on this limestone coast, gives a dry, bitter-edged, saline white.

sites.name: Stari Grad Plain, Hvar
sites.text: Greek colonists from Paros founded Pharos in 384 BC and divided the fertile plain into rectangular plots bounded by stone walls. Those plots are still farmed with vines and olives 2,400 years later, and the plain has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2008.

sites.name: Vis island
sites.text: Vis, ancient Issa, was a Greek colony from the 4th century BC and later a closed military island until 1989. Its white Vugava and the red Plavac Mali grow in the island's interior fields.

sites.name: Bucavac, Primošten
sites.text: The vineyards above Primošten are a lacework of tiny plots carved out of bare limestone and walled with the stones removed to plant them. They are famous for Babić. A photograph of them is said to have hung in the UN headquarters as a monument to human labour.

sites.name: Ponikve plateau, Pelješac
sites.text: The karst plateau of Ponikve above Ston at the neck of Pelješac became Croatia's 17th wine PDO in 2021, for Plavac Mali, Pošip and Maraština, including wine from raisined grapes.

sites.name: Kutjevo castle and the 1232 cellar
sites.text: Cistercian monks built the Kutjevo cellar in 1232. The baroque manor beside it later belonged to the Jesuits and then the Turković family, who began the wine archive in the late 19th century. Kutjevo's archive now holds over 65,000 bottles, the oldest a 1947 Pinot Blanc.

sites.name: Ilok Old Cellar (Iločki podrumi)
sites.text: Beneath Ilok castle on the Danube, the Old Cellar dates to 1450. Its 1947 Traminac is said to have been served at Queen Elizabeth II's coronation in 1953. Looted during the 1991 to 1998 occupation, it was restored and is again the heart of Iločki podrumi.

sites.name: Erdut
sites.text: Erdutski vinogradi works several hundred hectares on the loess bluff of Erdut above the Danube, where a medieval tower watches over the vines. Its cellar holds one of the largest oak casks in Europe.

sites.name: Momjan
sites.text: A hilltop village above Buje in north-west Istria, Momjan gives its name to the Muškat momjanski PDO (2021). Kozlović's winery sits in the valley below, among some of Istria's best Malvazija sites.

sites.name: Motovun
sites.text: The walled hill town of Motovun overlooks the Mirna valley, with Malvazija and Teran vineyards on its slopes and truffle oak forests below. Roxanich and other estates are nearby.

sites.name: Plešivica wine road
sites.text: The Plešivica hills near Jastrebarsko are lined with family wineries making traditional-method sparkling, Riesling and amphora wines. Tomac first buried qvevri-style amphorae here in the 2000s.
